title: PumpSense: Real-Time Detection and Target Extraction of Crypto Pump-and-Dumps on Telegram
summary: Cryptocurrency pump-and-dump schemes coordinated via Telegram threaten market integrity. However, existing research addressing this specific threat has not yet produced solutions that combine reliable results with fast response. This is in part due to the absence of publicly available, message-level labeled data, as well as design choices. In this paper, we address both issues. In particular, we introduce a corpus of over 280,000 Telegram posts from 39 pump-organizing groups, all manually reviewed to identify 2,246 pump announcements and their targeted cryptocurrency and exchange. Leveraging this dataset, we define two tasks: real-time pump-announcement detection and target cryptocurrency/exchange extraction. For detection, we compare two machine-learning models: a lightweight tree-based LightGBM classifier (F1=0.79, latency=9.4 s/sample) and a transformer-based BGE-M3 (F1=0.83, latency=50 ms/sample). With our proposed approach, we show that message analysis can achieve near-instant pump detection at the level of individual Telegram message windows. Unlike prior work that relies purely on market data and typically detects pumps tens of seconds after abnormal trading activity is observed, our method operates directly on the coordination messages themselves and can be evaluated in microseconds per window on commodity hardware. To our knowledge, we also establish the first benchmark for manipulated coin and exchange extraction. We demonstrate that traditional rule-based extraction methods, widely relied upon in prior literature, are ineffective due to ticker ambiguity. In contrast, LLMs achieve the highest accuracy with a score of 0.91.
core_methodology: The paper proposes using machine learning models (LightGBM and BGE-M3, a transformer-based embedding model) to detect pump-and-dump schemes in real-time by analyzing Telegram messages. It also explores the use of LLMs for extracting the target cryptocurrency and exchange from the messages. The key idea is to identify pump signals directly from communication channels *before* market data reflects the pump, thus gaining a timing advantage.
data_sources: The primary data source is a manually labeled dataset of over 280,000 Telegram posts from 39 pump-organizing groups, containing 2,246 pump announcements with identified target cryptocurrencies and exchanges.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the ability to front-run pump-and-dump schemes. By detecting the target cryptocurrency and exchange from Telegram messages *before* the price surge, a trader could potentially enter a position before the majority of the pump participants, capturing a significant portion of the upward price movement. Conversely, the information can also be used to short the cryptocurrency, or provide signals to exit existing long portfolios.
title_cn: PumpSense：基于Telegram的加密货币拉高抛售实时检测与目标提取
summary_cn: 该研究利用机器学习模型（LightGBM和Transformer）实时检测Telegram上的加密货币拉高抛售活动。通过分析社群消息，在市场价格异动前识别目标币种和交易所，从而获得交易先机。该方法可用于提前布局或规避风险，具有较高的alpha潜力。

title: Spectral Transformer Neural Processes
summary: Time series, spatial data, and images are natural applications of Neural Processes. However, when such data exhibit strong periodicity and quasi-periodicity, existing methods often suffer from underfitting and generalise poorly beyond the training distribution. In this work, we propose Spectral Transformer Neural Processes (STNPs), a frequency-aware extension of Transformer Neural Processes (TNPs). STNPs introduce a Spectral Aggregator that estimates an empirical context spectrum, compresses it into a spectral mixture, samples task-adaptive spectral features, and concatenates them with time-domain embeddings, thereby injecting a spectral-mixture-kernel bias into TNPs. This design reshapes the similarity geometry, allowing inputs that are distant in Euclidean space to remain close in an induced periodic manifold while enhancing time-frequency interactions. Extensive experiments on synthetic regression tasks, real-world time-series datasets, and an image dataset demonstrate that STNPs consistently improve predictive performance over existing baselines, extending Neural Processes beyond translation equivariance towards effective modelling of periodicity and quasi-periodicity.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Spectral Transformer Neural Processes (STNPs), an extension of Transformer Neural Processes (TNPs) that incorporates a Spectral Aggregator to model periodicity and quasi-periodicity in time series data. The Spectral Aggregator estimates the context spectrum, compresses it into a spectral mixture, and samples task-adaptive spectral features, which are then combined with time-domain embeddings. This helps the model capture frequency information and improve performance when dealing with periodic data.
data_sources: The paper uses synthetic regression tasks, real-world time-series datasets (unspecified in the abstract), and an image dataset. It mentions the model's applicability to spatial data as well.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improved forecasting and anomaly detection for financial time series. Many financial time series, such as trading volumes, volatility, and even asset prices, exhibit periodic or quasi-periodic behavior. STNPs could potentially capture these patterns more effectively than traditional methods, leading to more accurate predictions and the identification of profitable trading opportunities related to volatility, momentum, or mean reversion strategies. Improved modeling of seasonality is also a potential application.
title_cn: 频谱Transformer神经过程
summary_cn: 该论文提出频谱Transformer神经过程（STNPs），通过引入频谱聚合器来建模时间序列中的周期性和准周期性。 STNPs可能提升金融时间序列预测和异常检测能力，捕捉交易量、波动率和资产价格等周期性模式，从而改进波动率、动量或均值回复交易策略的预测准确性。

title: FinMoji: A Framework for Emoji-driven Sentiment Analysis in Financial Social Media
summary: This paper explores the use of emojis in financial sentiment analysis, focusing on the social media platform StockTwits. Emojis, increasingly prevalent in digital communication, have potential as compact indicators of investor sentiment, which can be critical for predicting market trends. Our study examines whether emojis alone can serve as reliable proxies for financial sentiment and how they compare with traditional text-based analysis. We conduct a series of experiments using logistic regression and transformer models. We further analyze the performance, computational efficiency, and data requirements of emoji-based versus text-based sentiment classification. Using a balanced dataset of about 528,000 emoji-containing StockTwits posts, we find that emoji-only models achieve F1 approximately 0.75, lower than text-emoji combined models, which achieve F1 approximately 0.88, but with far lower computational cost. This is a useful feature in time-sensitive settings such as high-frequency trading. Furthermore, certain emojis and emoji pairs exhibit strong predictive power for market sentiment, demonstrating over 90 percent accuracy in predicting bullish or bearish trends. Finally, our research reveals large statistical differences in emoji usage between financial and general social media contexts, stressing the need for domain-specific sentiment analysis models.
core_methodology: The paper uses logistic regression and transformer models to classify financial sentiment based on emojis in social media posts (StockTwits). It compares the performance, computational efficiency, and data requirements of emoji-based versus text-based sentiment analysis. Key focus on identifying emojis and emoji pairs with strong predictive power for bullish or bearish trends.
data_sources: StockTwits posts containing emojis (balanced dataset of approximately 528,000 posts).
alpha_potential: The alpha potential arises from the ability to rapidly gauge market sentiment using computationally efficient emoji-based models, particularly in high-frequency trading contexts. The identified emojis and emoji pairs with >90% accuracy in predicting market trends can be incorporated into sentiment-driven trading strategies or used as a feature in more complex models. The domain-specific nature of emoji usage in financial contexts can further enhance the signal's effectiveness.
title_cn: FinMoji：金融社交媒体中基于表情符号的情感分析框架
summary_cn: 本文提出了一种利用表情符号进行金融情感分析的方法，特别是在StockTwits平台上。研究发现，单独使用表情符号的模型虽然不如文本和表情符号结合的模型准确（F1约为0.75 vs 0.88），但计算成本更低，适合高频交易等对时间敏感的场景。某些表情符号或组合能够以超过90%的准确率预测市场情绪，具有潜在的alpha价值。可用于构建基于情绪的快速交易策略。

title: Cross-Cultural Transfer of Emoji Semantics and Sentiment in Financial Social Media
summary:
Emojis are widely used in online financial communication, but it is unclear whether they provide transferable sentiment signals across languages, platforms, and asset communities. This study examines the extent to which emoji usage, semantics, and sentiment polarity remain stable across financial communities, and how these layers influence zero-shot sentiment transfer. Using large corpora of Twitter and StockTwits posts in four languages, we measure cross-community divergence and evaluate sentiment models trained under emoji-only, text-only, and text+emoji inputs.
  We find that emoji frequencies differ across communities, especially across languages, but their semantics and sentiment polarity are largely stable. Cross-asset transferability shows minimal degradation, while cross-language transfer remains the most challenging. Including emojis consistently reduces transfer gaps relative to text-only models. These results indicate that financial communication exhibits a partially shared ``emoji code,'' and that emojis provide compact, language-independent sentiment cues that improve model generalization across markets and platforms.
core_methodology: The paper uses statistical analysis to quantify the stability of emoji semantics and sentiment polarity across different financial communities (languages, platforms, assets). It trains sentiment models using emoji-only, text-only, and combined inputs, comparing their performance in zero-shot sentiment transfer scenarios to assess the value of emojis as language-independent sentiment cues.
data_sources: Twitter and StockTwits posts in four languages, representing different financial communities.
alpha_potential: The research suggests that emojis can be used to improve sentiment analysis in financial social media, particularly when dealing with cross-lingual or cross-asset applications. This could potentially be incorporated into sentiment-based trading strategies, providing a more robust and generalized sentiment signal. The insight of stable emoji sentiment can be used to improve the signal-to-noise ratio in current sentiment classification models which drive trading decisions. Such models might be used to, for example, predict short term price movements based on public sentiment.
title_cn: 金融社交媒体中表情符号语义和情感的跨文化转移
summary_cn: 该研究发现表情符号在不同语言和金融社区中具有相对稳定的语义和情感极性。通过训练包含表情符号的 sentiment 模型，可以提升跨语言和跨资产的 sentiment 迁移学习效果，为建立更普适且稳健的基于社交媒体情感的量化交易策略提供理论依据，可用于改进现有模型，提升信噪比。

title: GravityGraphSAGE: Link Prediction in Directed Attributed Graphs
summary: Link prediction (inferring missing or future connections between nodes in a graph) is a fundamental problem in network science with widespread applications in, e.g., biological systems, recommender systems, finance and cybersecurity. The ability to accurately predict links has significant real-world applications, such as detecting fraudulent financial transactions or identifying drug-target interactions in biomedicine. Despite a rich literature, link prediction is still challenging, especially for graphs enriched with information on edges (direction) and nodes (attributes). In fact, research on link prediction, especially the one based on Graph Deep Learning (GDL), has mostly focused on undirected graphs, without fully leveraging node attributes. Here, we fill this gap by proposing Gravity-GraphSAGE (GG-SAGE), a modified version of GraphSAGE, a GDL model for node embeddings, composed of a gravity-inspired decoder. This implementation is the first example in the literature of a GraphSAGE backbone adopted for directed link prediction. Using the benchmark datasets Cora, Citeseer, PubMed and 16 real-world graphs from the online Netzschleuder repository, we show that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art GDL link prediction techniques. Using further experimental evidence, we relate the quality of the output of our model with various characteristics of the graph, suggesting that our framework scales well when applied to data of increasing complexity.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Gravity-GraphSAGE (GG-SAGE), a modified GraphSAGE model for link prediction in directed attributed graphs. It uses a gravity-inspired decoder on top of GraphSAGE embeddings. The core idea is to leverage both node attributes and edge direction to improve the accuracy of link prediction, particularly in scenarios where connections are not random.
data_sources: The paper uses benchmark datasets (Cora, Citeseer, PubMed) and 16 real-world graphs from the Netzschleuder repository. The key is the applicability to real-world directed attributed graphs; financial transaction networks or order book message flow networks are implicit candidates.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in identifying relationships between financial entities (e.g., accounts, institutions, transactions) that are not immediately obvious. For example, detecting fraudulent transactions by identifying unusual connections or predicting order flow by linking related order book events based on message content or participant identities. The ability to predict potential links could provide an early warning signal or allow for strategic positioning in the market. Especially important would be using the attributes (data) attached to the nodes/transactions themselves, not just network structure.
title_cn: GravityGraphSAGE: 有向属性图中的链接预测
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种改进的图神经网络模型GravityGraphSAGE，用于预测有向属性图中的链接。该模型适用于金融领域，可以用于识别欺诈交易、预测订单流，通过分析交易网络中不寻常的连接来提前预警或进行市场战略布局。关键在于利用节点属性和边方向进行更精准的预测。

title: Beyond ESG Scores: Learning Dynamic Constraints for Sequential Portfolio Optimization
summary: ESG-aware portfolio optimization is increasingly important for sustainable capital allocation, yet most learning-based methods still operationalize ESG by appending static scores to the policy observation or reward. This creates a mismatch for sequential control: ESG scores are noisy, provider-dependent, low-frequency, and temporally misaligned with sequential portfolio decisions, while financial evidence suggests that ESG is better treated as a portfolio preference, risk-exposure, or hedge dimension than as a robust alpha factor. We propose to impose ESG constraints without modifying the financial policy's observation or reward, using a Multimodal Action-Conditioned Constraint Field (MACF) that learns mechanism-specific ESG costs from point-in-time multimodal evidence and contemplated portfolio transitions. We then introduce MACF-X, a family of optimizer-specific adapters that converts MACF costs and uncertainties into native constrained-optimization interfaces through a shared slack- and uncertainty-aware pressure layer. Across multiple constraint-integration interfaces, MACF-X reduces tail ESG budget pressure while maintaining competitive financial performance. Ablations show that this improvement depends on dynamic evidence inputs and three-head decomposition, while static ESG-score proxies are nearly indistinguishable from score-shuffled noise baselines.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a Multimodal Action-Conditioned Constraint Field (MACF) and its optimizer-specific adapter MACF-X. MACF learns ESG costs from multimodal evidence and portfolio transitions, imposing dynamic ESG constraints on portfolio optimization without modifying the financial policy's observation or reward. MACF-X converts these costs into constrained-optimization interfaces using a slack- and uncertainty-aware pressure layer. The core idea is to treat ESG considerations as portfolio constraints rather than direct alpha signals, leading to potentially more robust strategies.
data_sources: The abstract mentions 'point-in-time multimodal evidence' without specifying the exact data. This implies a potential use of ESG scores from different providers, news sentiment, fundamental data, and potentially other alternative data sources relevant to ESG.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improved ESG compliance without sacrificing financial performance. By dynamically adapting to ESG considerations through constraints, the model avoids the pitfalls of treating static ESG scores as direct alpha sources, which can be noisy and unreliable. The potential 'alpha' comes from better risk-adjusted returns in the presence of ESG mandates, a more consistent implementation of an ESG investment thesis, and potentially the ability to dynamically exploit mispricings in ESG assessments across various data providers.
title_cn: 超越ESG评分：学习序列投资组合优化的动态约束
summary_cn: 该论文提出MACF和MACF-X模型，通过多模态数据动态学习ESG约束，而非直接使用静态ESG评分优化投资组合。该方法将ESG视为投资组合约束而非直接alpha来源，可能在满足ESG目标的同时提高风险调整回报。这对于需要考虑ESG因素的量化交易策略具有实际应用价值。

title: Hierarchical Attention-based Graph Neural Network with Relevance-driven Pruning
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel at relational reasoning but face two persistent challenges: the lack of interpretable attribution for heterogeneous node types, and the computational overhead of message passing over large, noisy graphs. We propose the Hierarchical Attention-based Heterogeneous GNN (HA-HeteroGNN), a framework that addresses both issues through a unied explainability-to-pruning pipeline. A two-tier attention mechanism separates sensor-level and context-level computation across 16 node types and 18 edge types, producing per-node relevance scores via an attention-based GNN Explainer without requiring gradient backpropagation. These relevance scores then serve as a principled pruning criterion: removing nodes identied as consistently uninformative yields a 27% reduction in graph edges while simultaneously improving classication accuracy by 2.46.1% across all model variants, challenging the conventional assumption that pruning necessarily trades accuracy for eciency. Experiments on a 50,000-record synthetic dataset spanning 11 report categories demonstrate 97.5% cross-strategy explanation stability and domain consistent sensor attribution, with training-time reductions of up to 43.9% and real-time inference latency of approximately 5860 ms per sample.
core_methodology: The paper presents a Hierarchical Attention-based Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HA-HeteroGNN) designed for explainable and efficient graph processing. It uses a two-tier attention mechanism across different node and edge types to generate relevance scores. These scores are then used to prune less informative nodes and edges, leading to improved classification accuracy and reduced computational cost. The approach enables better understanding of node importance and faster inference by removing redundant information from the graph.
data_sources: The paper uses a synthetic dataset with 50,000 records structured across 16 node types, 18 edge types, and 11 report categories. While the dataset is synthetic, the structure aims to mimic real-world relational data.
alpha_potential: The methodology could be adapted to financial markets by representing assets, companies, or other financial entities as nodes in a graph. Relationships (e.g., correlations, supply chain connections, ownership) would be edges. The attention mechanism can potentially identify key drivers of asset behavior or systemic risk. Pruning can help reduce noise and feature selection when constructing features for trading algorithms. By generating relevance scores for different nodes and edges, this method facilitates factor selection and better understanding of feature importance in quantitative models. Furthermore, identifying and removing less informative nodes and edges can potentially improve the performance of existing trading signals and reduce backtesting time.
title_cn: 基于层级注意力机制的图神经网络与相关性驱动的剪枝
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种基于层级注意力机制的异构图神经网络(HA-HeteroGNN)，用于提高图处理的可解释性和效率。 通过节点和边类型上的两级注意力机制，生成可用于修剪信息量较少的节点和边的相关性分数，提高分类精度并降低计算成本。 在应用于金融市场时，这种方法可以帮助识别资产行为的关键驱动因素、量化模型的特征选择或降低系统风险。

title: The Engineering of Skew: A Path-Dependent Framework for Asymmetric Volatility Management
summary: Volatility is the language in which finance often describes risk, but it is not the language in which institutions experience risk. Allocators live through drawdowns, liquidity needs, spending rules, rebalance decisions, board oversight, and the interval between a prior high-water mark and full recovery. This paper develops a path-dependent framework for asymmetric volatility management. The arithmetic of recovery is nonlinear: after a drawdown of depth $D$, the required gain is $R=\frac{1}{1-D}-1$. Lower volatility can improve geometric compounding through the familiar small-return approximation $g \approx μ-\frac{1}{2}σ^2$, but symmetric de-risking can also impair recovery if it sacrifices too much upside participation. The relevant design problem is therefore not volatility reduction in isolation; it is conditional exposure shaping. Skew engineering is defined here as the portfolio construction discipline of reducing harmful downside participation more than productive upside participation, controlling submergence, and preserving enough recovery participation to sustain compounding under adverse regimes. The resulting Recovery-Efficiency Protocol links drawdown depth, time underwater, recovery burden reduction, and rebound participation into an allocator-facing reporting discipline. Machine learning and AI methods are framed as tools for conditional estimation, regime mapping, robustness testing, and model-risk governance, not as market prediction.
core_methodology: The paper proposes a path-dependent framework for managing asymmetric volatility, focusing on 'skew engineering'. It emphasizes conditional exposure shaping to reduce downside participation more than upside, aiming to improve recovery efficiency after drawdowns. The core idea is to link drawdown depth, time underwater, recovery burden reduction, and rebound participation. Machine learning is suggested for conditional estimation and regime mapping, not for direct market prediction.
data_sources: The paper doesn't specify particular data sources, but it implicitly assumes access to price data to calculate drawdowns and volatility. It would be suitable for any asset class where drawdown management is a concern.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in more efficiently navigating drawdowns and improving long-term geometric returns by selectively participating in upside moves while limiting downside exposure. By dynamically adjusting portfolio skew based on drawdown levels and market regimes, the strategy could outperform benchmarks that don't explicitly manage path-dependent risk. The 'Recovery-Efficiency Protocol' provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of this approach.
title_cn: 偏度工程：非对称波动管理的路径依赖框架
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种路径依赖型的非对称波动管理框架，侧重于通过选择性地降低下跌参与度并保留上涨潜力，来提高回撤后的复苏效率。核心在于根据回撤深度和市场状态动态调整投资组合的偏度，利用机器学习进行情景估计和状态识别，而非直接预测市场，从而优化长期几何收益。

title: Fin-Bias: Comprehensive Evaluation for LLM Decision-Making under human bias in Finance Domain
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in financial contexts, raising critical concerns about reliability, alignment, and susceptibility to adversarial manipulation. While prior finance-related benchmarks assess LLMs' capabilities in stock trading, they are often restricted to small sample and fail to demonstrate LLM susceptibility to context with potential human bias. We introduce Fin-Bias (financial herding under long and uncertain financial context), a benchmark for evaluating LLM investment decision-making when faced with uncertainty and possible human-biased opinions. Fin-Bias includes 8868 long firm-specific analyst reports, including firm aspects summarized and analyzed by sophisticated analysts with investment ratings (Bullish/Neutral/Bearish) spanning from various industries. We present large language models with firm analyst reports with/without analyst investment ratings and even with 'fake' rating, to get investment ratings generated by LLMs. Our results reveal that LLMs tend to herd the explicit bias in context. We also develop a method to detect potential human opinions, which can encourage LLMs to think independently, some models even exceed human performance in predicting future stock return.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Fin-Bias, a benchmark using analyst reports to evaluate how LLMs make investment decisions under uncertainty and potential human biases embedded in the reports and analyst ratings. It then proposes a method to detect and mitigate these biases, potentially leading LLMs to generate more independent and accurate investment ratings.
data_sources: 8868 firm-specific analyst reports including firm aspects summarized and analyzed by professionals with investment ratings (Bullish/Neutral/Bearish).
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in using LLMs to analyze analyst reports, identify and filter out human biases embedded within the reports and analyst ratings, and generate independent investment ratings that potentially outperform human analysts by better predicting future stock returns. This can be integrated into trading strategies that are contrarian to consensus analyst opinions or that capitalize on the improved predictive power of unbiased LLM assessments.
title_cn: Fin-Bias：金融领域人类偏见下LLM决策的综合评估
summary_cn: 本文提出了Fin-Bias基准，利用分析师报告评估LLM在不确定性和潜在偏见下的投资决策能力。通过检测和消除报告中的人类偏见，LLM有望生成更独立、准确的投资评级，从而用于构建收益更高的量化交易策略，例如反共识交易或基于更准确LLM评级的套利策略。

title: ChaosNetBench: Benchmarking Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks on Chaotic Lattice Dynamics
summary: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) are widely used for short-term forecasting in dynamic physical systems such as traffic and weather. However, the prevailing evaluation practice uses real world benchmark data sets in a single domain with a single fixed holdout splits, making it difficult to compare architectures across different dynamical regimes. We introduce ChaosNetBench (CNB), a synthetic benchmark dataset and evaluation framework for studying STGNN performance under controlled multidimensional chaotic dynamics. CNB is built on a lattice of coupled standard maps with independently tunable local chaos ($K$), coupling strength ($\varepsilon$), and system size ($N$), providing known topology and known dynamics across 96 system instances and 9{,}600 trajectories. We introduce chaos indicators, evaluation metrics and a protocol to analyze and compare the capacity of STGNN architectures to deal with different levels of local and global chaos. We illustrate the usage of the framework by analyzing 13 architectures (5 STGNNs and 8 non-graph baselines). The results reveal a regime dependent transition in which non-graph baselines (TCN, N-BEATS, iTransformer) remain competitive when there is low local chaos, while STGNNs (e.g., Graph WaveNet, D2STGNN, STAEformer) are generally more resilient to higher levels of local and global chaos. CNB provides a practical, reusable testbed for systematically comparing and analyzing the capacity of STGNN architectures to handle different levels of local and global chaos.
core_methodology: The paper introduces ChaosNetBench (CNB), a synthetic benchmark dataset and evaluation framework using coupled standard maps to study Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (STGNN) performance under multidimensional chaotic dynamics. It provides tunable local chaos, coupling strength, and system size, enabling controlled experiments on STGNNs. It benchmarks STGNNs and non-graph models to understand their robustness to different chaos levels.
data_sources: Synthetic data generated from coupled standard maps with tunable parameters to simulate chaotic systems.
alpha_potential: The paper provides a controlled environment to develop and test STGNNs capable of forecasting complex dynamic systems. This can potentially lead to identifying patterns or predicting regime changes in financial markets exhibiting chaotic behavior. Specific alpha generation would still require financial data training, but this benchmark helps pre-select robust models.
title_cn: ChaosNetBench：时空图神经网络在混沌格子动力学上的基准测试
summary_cn: 该论文提出的ChaosNetBench是一个合成数据集，用于评估时空图神经网络（STGNN）在混沌动力系统中的性能。 通过控制混沌程度，研究STGNN和传统模型预测能力。 这有助于量化交易员选择更稳健的STGNN模型，以应对金融市场中潜在的混沌行为和复杂动态。

title: LLM-Driven Performance-Space Augmentation for Meta-Learning-Based Algorithm Selection
summary: Meta-learning for algorithm selection relies on a meta-dataset in which each row corresponds to a supervised learning dataset described by meta-features and labelled with a target value that is associated with algorithm choice (typically, some function of algorithm performance). A persistent limitation is that the number of curated real-world datasets is small, resulting in sparse meta-datasets that constrain meta-learner generalisation. In this paper, we address this problem by augmenting the meta-dataset with synthetic regression datasets produced via a large language model (LLM), with generation steered toward target regions of a low-dimensionality performance space. In our experiments, we adopt a two-dimensional geometric setting defined by the cross-validated $R^2$ scores of two anchor algorithms, known as landmarkers. We compare two augmentation strategies: (1) uniform sampling, which distributes synthetic datasets across the performance space; and (2) margin-based sampling, which concentrates them near the decision boundary where landmarker preference is most ambiguous. Across 42 real-world UCI regression datasets and 730 synthetic datasets, both strategies substantially improve meta-learner performance over the unaugmented baseline under regression and multi-label evaluation formulations. However, uniform augmentation consistently outperforms margin-based augmentation, achieving a 17.47% relative reduction in Hamming loss, a 100.41% relative improvement in subset accuracy, and a +6.09% relative gain in pooled out-of-fold $R^2$. These results lead us to postulate a central thesis: the performance of algorithms resides on a low-dimensional performance manifold, whose reconstruction bias may be minimised by user-guided LLMs that seek to maximise uniform $ε$-cover, and consequently, lead to improved meta-learning for algorithm selection.
core_methodology: The paper uses LLMs to generate synthetic datasets to augment meta-learning models for algorithm selection. The meta-learning task aims to predict the best algorithm (from a set of pre-defined algorithms) for a given regression task, based on meta-features of the datasets. The synthetic data is generated to cover the performance space of 'landmarker' algorithms (anchor algorithms). The effectiveness of augmentation is evaluated by improvements in meta-learner performance in selecting the best algorithm across real-world regression datasets.
data_sources: Real-world UCI regression datasets are used, along with synthetically generated regression datasets produced by the LLM. The performance of pre-defined algorithms on these datasets provides the target variable for training the meta-learner.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in dynamically selecting algorithms best suited for a particular trading environment. The paper addresses the cold-start problem of meta-learning by generating synthetic data. In trading, this could mean adapting to regime changes or new market dynamics by choosing parameter settings (or entirely new models) on the fly that are likely to perform best on current patterns. Instead of generating data, the LLM could generate market simulations which feed into the algorithm selection process. Applying it to portfolio optimization also holds value: select optimal strategies for asset allocation.

title: Optimal Regret for Single Index Bandits
summary:
We study the $\textit{single-index bandit}$ problem, where rewards depend on an unknown one-dimensional projection of high-dimensional contexts through an unknown reward function. This model extends linear and generalized linear bandits to a nonparametric setting, and is particularly relevant when the reward function is not known in advance. While optimal regret guarantees are known for monotone reward functions, the general non-monotone case remains poorly understood, with the best known bound being $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ (under standard boundedness and Lipschitz assumptions on the reward function [Kang et al., 2025]).
  We close this gap by establishing the optimal regret for general single-index bandits. We propose a simple two-phase algorithm, namely, Zoomed Single Index Bandit with Upper Confidence Bound ($\texttt{ZoomSIB-UCB}$), that first estimates the projection direction via a normalized Stein estimator, and then reduces the problem to a one-dimensional bandit using discretization and finally use UCB. This approach achieves a regret of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$, and improves significantly upon prior work without any additional assumptions. We also prove a matching minimax lower bound of $\tildeΩ(T^{2/3})$, showing that the upper bound is essentially tight. Our upper and lower bounds together provide a sharp characterization of the regret in single-index bandits. Moreover, the empirical results further demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a novel algorithm, Zoomed Single Index Bandit with Upper Confidence Bound (ZoomSIB-UCB), for solving single-index bandit problems. This algorithm operates in two phases: first, it estimates the projection direction using a normalized Stein estimator; second, it reduces the problem to a one-dimensional bandit through discretization and applies UCB. The core idea is to efficiently explore and exploit the reward function in a high-dimensional context with an unknown one-dimensional projection.
data_sources: The paper doesn't specify specific financial data. However, in principle this algortihm or variants thereof could apply to many situations which can be formulated as a multi-armed bandit, selecting from many features, regimes, asset pairs etc.
alpha_potential: The algorithm can potentially be used for adaptive trading strategy selection. For example, the contexts could represent market conditions or asset features, the single-index projection could represent an unknown factor, and the reward represents profit/loss. The algorithm could be employed to dynamically choose the most effective trading strategy or asset allocation based on the estimated single-index, enabling exploitation of time-varying market dynamics and potentially capturing non-linear relationships between features and returns. This is especially useful where the reward function is not known in advance or changes over time.

title: Tabular Foundation Model for Generative Modelling
summary: Generative modelling is a demanding test of foundation models, because it requires robust, holistic representation learning for a given data modality, rather than optimisation for a supervised prediction target alone. While recent work on tabular foundation models has achieved remarkable progress in predictive modelling, generative tabular foundation models remain underexplored. Existing tabular foundation generators, in particular, have not yet consistently matched strong dataset-specific generators in synthetic data quality. A key reason is their misalignment with the distinctive causal structural prior of heterogeneous tabular data. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a novel tabular foundation model, \textbf{TabFORGE}, built on pretrained \textbf{Tab}ular \textbf{FO}undational \textbf{R}epresentations for \textbf{GE}neration. TabFORGE is designed to utilise the implicitly learned causal information underlying diverse tabular datasets in a unified latent space induced by a pretrained causality-aware feature encoder. It further decouples latent modelling from decoding through a two-stage design: we first pretrain a score-based diffusion transformer, and then pretrain a denoising-aligned decoder using the denoised latent embeddings. This design elegantly mitigates the distribution shifts in latent embeddings that typically arise between training and inference. We evaluate TabFORGE comprehensively against 22 benchmark methods on 45 real-world datasets. Our results show that TabFORGE effectively learns and leverages generalisable tabular representations, enabling efficient generation of high-quality synthetic tabular data, particularly with strong structural fidelity.
core_methodology: TabFORGE is a two-stage generative tabular foundation model. It uses a pretrained causality-aware feature encoder to learn latent representations of tabular data. A score-based diffusion transformer models the latent space, and a denoising-aligned decoder generates synthetic tabular data from the denoised latent embeddings, mitigating distribution shifts.

alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in using TabFORGE to generate synthetic financial data with preserved causal relationships. This synthetic data can augment limited historical data, improve the robustness of backtesting, or train machine learning models in data-scarce environments like predicting rare events such as defaults or extreme market movements. It can also create 'what-if' scenarios by modifying the synthetic data.

title: From Passive Reuse to Active Reasoning: Grounding Large Language Models for Neuro-Symbolic Experience Replay
summary: While experience replay is essential for data efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL), standard methods treat the replay buffer as a passive memory system, prioritizing samples based on numerical prediction errors rather than their semantic significance. This approach stands in contrast to human learning, which accelerates mastery by actively abstracting fragmented experiences into behavioral rules. To bridge this gap, we propose Neuro-Symbolic Experience Replay (NSER), a framework that transforms experience replay from a passive sample reuse mechanism into an active engine for knowledge construction. Specifically, NSER addresses the incompatibility between linguistic reasoning and numerical optimization through a novel neuro-symbolic grounding pipeline. It leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) in a zero-shot manner to induce candidate behavioral rules from accumulated trajectories, grounds these insights into differentiable first-order logic representations, and utilizes the resulting symbolic structures to dynamically reweight the replay distribution. By allowing abstract knowledge to directly shape policy optimization, NSER achieves consistent superior sample efficiency and convergence speed across reactive, rule-based, and procedural benchmarks.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Neuro-Symbolic Experience Replay (NSER), which enhances reinforcement learning by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) for abstracting experiences into behavioral rules. It leverages LLMs to induce candidate rules from trajectories, grounds these rules into differentiable first-order logic, and uses the symbolic structures to dynamically reweight the replay distribution, guiding policy optimization.
data_sources: The paper uses reactive, rule-based, and procedural benchmarks. To apply this in finance, relevant data sources could include historical market data (price, volume, order book), news sentiment, economic indicators, and potentially proprietary datasets representing market participant behavior.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in more efficient and adaptive reinforcement learning agents. By actively structuring and reweighting experiences, agents can learn more quickly and effectively exploit market inefficiencies compared to standard RL algorithms. This can lead to better execution strategies, faster adaptation to changing market conditions, or identification of novel trading opportunities by extracting rules that represent profitable patterns unrecognized by traditional methods.

title: Let the Target Select for Itself: Data Selection via Target-Aligned Paths
summary: Targeted data selection aims to identify training samples from a large candidate pool that improve performance on a specific downstream task. Many recent methods estimate candidate utility by aggregating local attribution scores along a trajectory induced by the candidate pool. When the pool is heterogeneous, however, this reference trajectory may be misaligned with the dynamics of a target-aligned selected subset, creating what we call reference path bias. We propose an alternative reference path: a validation-induced flow obtained from a short, capacity-limited warmup on the available target validation proxy. Along this path, candidates are scored by a normalized endpoint loss drop, yielding a simple zero-order selection rule that requires no candidate gradients or Hessian approximations. Across controlled logistic, vision, and instruction-tuning experiments, this score is competitive with strong dynamic attribution baselines while substantially reducing warmup and storage cost. Moreover, since the reference trajectory is decoupled from any specific candidate pool, the same compact warmup can be reused across additional pools without recomputing the trajectory.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a novel data selection method called 'Target-Aligned Paths' for improving the performance of machine learning models. It addresses the 'reference path bias' in existing methods by using a validation-induced flow as a reference path for scoring candidate data points. This flow is obtained by a short warmup on a target validation proxy, and candidates are scored by the normalized endpoint loss drop. This is a zero-order selection rule without gradient or Hessian approximations.
data_sources: The paper focuses on controlled experiments in logistic regression, vision, and instruction-tuning, but the underlying concept could apply to financial data where large and heterogeneous datasets exist.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in its potential to improve the efficiency of model training by selecting the most relevant data points. In financial markets, this could be used to identify specific historical periods or market regimes that are most informative for predicting future price movements. For example, within a large universe of stock data (including fundamental and alternative data) or high-frequency limit order book data, this selection method could focus on data most informative for specific trading styles like momentum or volatility arbitrage. It could also be applied to select relevant news articles for sentiment analysis in NLP-driven trading strategies.

title: Universal Feature Selection with Noisy Observations and Weak Symmetry Conditions
summary: This paper relaxes the restrictive symmetry conditions adopted in [4], [5] and extends their universal feature selection framework to accommodate noisy observations as well as attribute structures that may exhibit directional preferences. We introduce the notion of weak spherical symmetry, quantified by second-moment distances, which allows controlled deviations from rotational invariance. Under this relaxed condition, we develop a universal feature selection framework based on the singular value decomposition of the canonical dependence matrix computed from noisy data. Our main result shows that the selected features achieve asymptotically optimal error exponents up to a residual term that depends on the symmetry deviation $δ$ and the noise levels $η_1, η_2$. When $δ, η_1, η_2$ are relatively small, our result recovers that of [5], thereby demonstrating that exact spherical symmetry is unnecessary. Overall, our findings highlight the robustness of the selection framework against second-moment deviations and observation noise, thereby broadening its applicability across diverse inference tasks and providing a theoretically grounded tool for universal feature selection in practical scenarios.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a universal feature selection framework based on the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the canonical dependence matrix, modified to accommodate noisy data and deviations from spherical symmetry (weak spherical symmetry). It quantifies symmetry deviation using second-moment distances and provides error bounds for feature selection under these relaxed conditions.
data_sources: The paper itself does not specify data sources, but the methodology is designed for noisy data and general attribute structures, implying it can be applied to a wide range of financial data, including market data (prices, volumes) and alternative data (sentiment, news). The key is that the method can handle noisy observations, which is inherent in practical finance.
alpha_potential: This method offers potential alpha generation through improved feature selection, particularly in situations where traditional methods might fail due to noise or violation of symmetry assumptions. In factor investing, noisy macroeconomic variables or alternative data can be better incorporated into models. In high-frequency trading, noisy order book data can be processed to identify critical order flow characteristics with more robustness. Improved feature selection also offers the chance for enhanced portfolio optimization and more reliable predictions, leading to superior risk-adjusted returns.

title: Empowering VLMs for Few-Shot Multimodal Time Series Classification via Tailored Agentic Reasoning
summary: In this paper, we propose the first VL$\underline{\textbf{M}}$ $\underline{\textbf{a}}$gentic $\underline{\textbf{r}}$easoning framework for few-$\underline{\textbf{s}}$hot multimodal $\underline{\textbf{T}}$ime $\underline{\textbf{S}}$eries $\underline{\textbf{C}}$lassification ($\textbf{MarsTSC}$), which introduces a self-evolving knowledge bank as a dynamic context iteratively refined via reflective agentic reasoning. The framework comprises three collaborative roles: i) Generator conducts reliable classification via reasoning; ii) Reflector diagnoses the root causes of reasoning errors to yield discriminative insights targeting the temporal features overlooked by Generator; iii) Modifier applies verified updates to the knowledge bank to prevent context collapse. We further introduce a test-time update strategy to enable cautious, continuous knowledge bank refinement to mitigate few-shot bias and distribution shift. Extensive experiments across 12 mainstream time series benchmarks demonstrate that $\textbf{MarsTSC}$ delivers substantial and consistent performance gains across 6 VLM backbones, outperforming both classical and foundation model-based time series baselines under few-shot conditions, while producing interpretable rationales that ground each classification decision in human-readable feature evidence.
core_methodology: The paper presents a VLM-agentic reasoning framework (MarsTSC) for few-shot multimodal time series classification. It utilizes three roles: a Generator for initial classification, a Reflector to diagnose reasoning errors and identify overlooked temporal features, and a Modifier to update a knowledge bank based on the Reflector's insights. A test-time update strategy further refines the knowledge bank. The key is the iteratively refined agentic reasoning and self-evolving knowledge bank for improved time series classification in low-data regimes.
data_sources: The paper evaluates the framework on 12 mainstream time series benchmarks, implying usage of standard time series datasets. However, specific financial datasets are not explicitly mentioned; thus it must be generalized financial time series data (e.g. stock prices, macroeconomic indicators).
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the framework's ability to effectively classify time series data in few-shot scenarios. This could be valuable in identifying patterns and making predictions for novel financial events or situations with limited historical data. The framework's interpretability, producing human-readable feature evidence, could also aid in understanding and validating trading signals.

title: Learning-Augmented Scalable Linear Assignment Problem Optimization via Neural Dual Warm-Starts
summary: The Linear Assignment Problem (LAP) is a fundamental combinatorial optimization task with applications ranging from computer vision to logistics. Classical exact solvers such as the Hungarian and Jonker-Volgenant (LAPJV) algorithms guarantee optimality, but their cubic time complexity $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ becomes a bottleneck for large-scale instances. Recent learning-based approaches aim to replace these solvers with neural models, often sacrificing exactness or failing to scale due to memory constraints. We propose a learning-augmented framework that accelerates exact assignment solvers while maintaining optimality and worst-case guarantees. Our method predicts dual variables to warm-start a classical solver, with a fallback that prevents asymptotic runtime degradation when the learned advice is unreliable. We introduce RowDualNet, a lightweight row-independent architecture that avoids the $\mathcal{O}(N^{2})$ memory bottleneck of graph-based models, enabling neural warm-starting at large scale ($N=16{,}384$). Feasibility is ensured via a constructive mechanism based on LP duality (namely, the Min-Trick), eliminating costly iterative projection. Empirically, our approach reduces the search effort of LAPJV and achieves over $2{\times}$ speedups on challenging synthetic distributions, in addition to improving over $1.25{\times}$ and $1.5{\times}$ on real-world tracking (MOT) and transportation (LPT) datasets, respectively, while strictly maintaining full optimality, effectively yielding a robust zero-shot generalization to real-world tasks.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a learning-augmented framework (RowDualNet) to accelerate Linear Assignment Problem (LAP) solvers. It predicts dual variables using a neural network to warm-start classical solvers like LAPJV, ensuring optimality and scalability. The Min-Trick is used to ensure feasibility. This reduces computational time while maintaining solution quality.
data_sources: The paper utilizes synthetic distributions and real-world datasets, specifically Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) and Logistics Planning Task (LPT). Although not financial, the underlying cost matrix structure may be translated to financial applications.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improving the efficiency of portfolio optimization or order execution algorithms that rely on solving LAP subproblems. For example, in optimal trade pairing given some constraints. Speeding up the optimization process allows for faster reaction to market changes and potentially better execution prices. Can also be applied to optimal matching of orders in a dark pool to increase liquidity and reduce adverse selection. Improvements would come from the lower computational cost.

title: Near-Optimal Last-Iterate Convergence for Zero-Sum Games with Bandit Feedback and Opponent Actions
summary:
Last-iterate convergence of learning dynamics in games has attracted significant recent attention. In two-player zero-sum games with bandit feedback, where only the loss of the selected action pair is observed, Fiegel et al. (2025) show a separation between average-iterate and last-iterate convergence in duality gap: while the optimal t^(-1/2) rate after t rounds is achievable for the former via standard no-regret algorithms, the latter cannot converge faster than t^(-1/3) in expectation or t^(-1/4) with high probability. However, in many practical settings, such as preference learning, the players observe not only their loss but also the opponent's action. This raises a natural question: can such additional information enable faster last-iterate convergence?
  We answer this question affirmatively, showing that t^(-1/2) last-iterate convergence is achievable with high probability in this setting, via an efficient algorithm that updates its strategy infrequently by solving an estimated log-barrier-regularized game. We identify fundamental obstacles preventing standard analysis for multi-armed bandits, the single-player case, from generalizing to games, and develop a novel analysis to overcome them. Experiments confirm that our algorithm indeed converges faster than naive baselines and prior methods that do not exploit opponent-action feedback. Finally, we note that our results also improve those for dueling bandits, a special case with skew-symmetric game matrices.
core_methodology: The paper develops an efficient algorithm based on solving an estimated log-barrier-regularized game in zero-sum games with bandit feedback and opponent actions. It achieves t^(-1/2) last-iterate convergence with high probability by infrequently updating its strategy. The core contribution lies in overcoming obstacles in generalizing multi-armed bandit analysis to games by developing a novel analysis technique.
data_sources: The paper's experimental section uses simulated data, which represents the loss incurred based on chosen action pairs, and the observed opponent actions. In a trading context, these "actions" could relate to order placement strategies, portfolio allocations, or market making decisions.
alpha_potential: The improved convergence rate for zero-sum games suggests potential applications in pairs trading, options market making, or any other financial setting that can be modeled as a zero-sum game. Observing the 'opponent' (market maker, other traders) actions and adapting strategies with faster convergence could lead to improved profitability by more quickly identifying and exploiting profitable opportunities. The model could perform better in non-stationary environments if the algo trains quickly. Dueling bandits improvement also can be applied to A/B testing of trading algos in live market conditions.

title: Skill-R1: Agent Skill Evolution via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic large language models often rely on skills, reusable natural language procedures that guide planning, action, and tool use. In practice, skills are typically improved through prompt engineering or by aligning the task LLM itself, which is costly, model-specific, and often infeasible for closed-source models. Skill optimization is not a one-step problem but a recurrent process with two coupled levels of credit assignment: a useful skill must improve rollout quality under current conditioning, while a useful revision must turn observed outcomes into a better skill for the next round. We propose Skill-R1, a reinforcement learning framework for instance-level recurrent skill optimization from verifiable rewards. Rather than updating the task LLM, Skill-R1 trains a lightweight skill generator that conditions on the task context, prior rollouts, and their verified outcomes to produce skills that steer a frozen task LLM. This preserves black-box compatibility with both open- and closed-source models while making adaptation substantially cheaper than model-level updates. Skill-R1 proceeds over multiple generations: at each step, the current skill induces rollouts whose verified outcomes are fed back to produce the next revision. To optimize this recurrent process, we introduce a bi-level group-relative policy optimization objective combining intra-generation and inter-generation advantages. The intra-generation term compares rollouts under shared skill conditioning, while the inter-generation term rewards revisions that improve behavior across successive generations. Together, these provide a principled objective for directional skill evolution rather than one-shot self-refinement. Empirically, Skill-R1 achieves consistent gains over no-skill baselines and standard GRPO across benchmarks with verifiable rewards, with particularly strong improvements on complex, multi-step tasks.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Skill-R1, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for optimizing agent skills (reusable natural language procedures) that guide a large language model (LLM) in tasks requiring planning, action, and tool use. It trains a lightweight skill generator that conditions on task context, prior rollouts, and verified outcomes to produce improved skills that steer a frozen (black-box) task LLM. The method employs a bi-level group-relative policy optimization objective combining intra-generation (comparing rollouts under shared skill sets) and inter-generation (rewarding skill revisions that improve behavior across generations) advantages to optimize the recurrent skill learning process.
data_sources: The paper focuses on generic benchmarks with verifiable rewards. While not explicitly finance-related, the abstract implies the use of simulated environments or tasks with clear outcome metrics.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in adapting LLMs for complex trading tasks where skills (specific task-oriented prompts and instruction sets) are dynamically optimized based on market feedback. This could be applied to areas like news sentiment analysis, automated report generation, or complex event processing, where an agent needs to interpret large quantities of information to create profitable trading decisions. The system's ability to iteratively improve the skill set based on verifiable rewards (e.g., profitability) could lead to consistently better execution than fixed or manually-tuned systems. This framework could be used for algorithmic order execution or for automating portions of fundamental research.

title: MC$^2$: Monte Carlo Correction for Fast Elliptic PDE Solving
summary: Partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin scientific computing, but real-world deployment is bounded by compute. Classical Monte Carlo solvers such as Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) are unbiased and geometry-agnostic but are slow. Learned solvers are fast but biased and brittle under distribution shift. We present \textbf{MC$^2$}, a hybrid WoS-Neural Network (WoS-NN) PDE solver that treats a low-budget Monte Carlo solution as a structured estimator of the true field and learns a single-pass neural correction to recover a high-fidelity solution. MC$^2$ matches the accuracy of solutions using over $1000\times$ more Monte Carlo compute, outperforming all evaluated classical, denoising, and neural-operator baselines. To enable reproducible study of finite-compute PDE solving, we additionally release \textbf{PDEZoo}, the largest standardized elliptic PDE benchmark to date: 2M PDEs spanning five elliptic families and unlimited geometric compositions, with analytic ground truth and multi-budget Monte Carlo trajectories. Together \textbf{MC$^2$} and \textbf{PDEZoo} (1) empirically establish that finite-sample Monte Carlo error is structured, learnable, and correctable in a single forward pass, (2) show that we can solve PDEs $\sim$\textbf{1000x} faster than with just WoS, and (3) provide the evaluation infrastructure the field has so far lacked.
core_methodology: The paper presents MC$^2$, a hybrid Monte Carlo and Neural Network solver for elliptic Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). It combines Walk-on-Spheres (WoS), a Monte Carlo method, with a neural network to correct the low-budget Monte Carlo solution. The neural network learns to estimate the error in the Monte Carlo solution and provides a correction to achieve a high-fidelity result with significantly reduced computation. They also release PDEZoo, a benchmark dataset for elliptic PDEs.
data_sources: PDEZoo: A synthetic dataset of 2M PDEs spanning five elliptic families and unlimited geometric compositions, with analytic ground truth and multi-budget Monte Carlo trajectories.
alpha_potential: The potential alpha stems from applying these improved PDE solvers to option pricing and derivatives modeling. Many option pricing models involve solving PDEs (e.g., Black-Scholes, Heston). MC$^2$ could significantly accelerate the pricing process or improve the accuracy of pricing complex derivatives, potentially uncovering arbitrage opportunities and improving hedging strategies. Specifically, improved pricing models for exotic options or instruments with complex payoff structures could yield improved trading performance.

title: First Worst-Case Regret Bounds for Combinatorial Thompson Sampling in Sleeping Semi-Bandits
summary: We revisit combinatorial Thompson sampling (CTS) for semi-bandits with sleeping arms, where arm availability varies over time and actions must satisfy combinatorial constraints, as in wireless mesh routing with fluctuating link availability. Despite its practical relevance, CTS has been hindered by several long-standing problems: (i) the absence of worst-case regret guarantees in the semi-bandit setting even without sleeping arms, (ii) the lack of theory under adversarially varying availability, and (iii) the consistently weak empirical performance of CTS with Gaussian priors (CTS-G). This paper resolves these long-standing issues by providing the first worst-case regret analysis of CTS-G, proving an upper bound of $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{NT})$ and a matching lower bound of $\tildeΩ(m\sqrt{NT})$. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we further propose CL-SG, a simple CTS-G variant that samples a single shared Gaussian seed each round to coordinate exploration across arms. We show that CL-SG achieves an improved regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{mNT})$, together with a matching lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{mNT})$. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that CL-SG consistently outperforms strong baselines including CTS-G and CTS-B, and we open-source our implementation for reproducibility.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a new variant of Combinatorial Thompson Sampling (CTS) called CL-SG, designed to address the limitations of standard CTS in semi-bandit settings with sleeping arms (varying arm availability). CL-SG uses a shared Gaussian seed to coordinate exploration across arms, achieving improved regret bounds. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of both CTS-G and CL-SG, including worst-case regret bounds and matching lower bounds. This methodology is built around reinforcement learning to make decisions in environments with combinatorial constraints and fluctuating availability.
data_sources: The experiments utilize real-world datasets, although the specific datasets are not detailed in the abstract. It can be inferred that the 'real-world datasets' capture some degree of time-varying availability (sleeping arms). To use this in a trading strategy, one would likely need to apply this to data where tradable assets (arms) temporarily become unavailable (e.g. due to liquidity constraints, trading halts, or order execution difficulties).
alpha_potential: The alpha potential stems from the ability to effectively manage combinatorial trading decisions (e.g., portfolio construction, execution of correlated orders) when certain assets or trading venues exhibit time-varying availability or temporary constraints. This is particularly relevant in markets with fragmented liquidity or where execution risks fluctuate. It could be adapted to optimal order routing, optimal portfolio construction under liquidity regimes, or even flash crash avoidance by dynamically updating weights based on execution probabilities.

title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multicalibration
summary: We study online multicalibration beyond the worst-case. We give a single, efficient algorithm which dynamically interpolates between benign and worst-case sequences by adaptively refining a dyadic grid of prediction values. Its error is controlled by the number of leaves in the refinement tree. Our analysis recovers the known $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ worst-case-optimal rate for online multicalibration, while simultaneously automatically adapting to easier instances: in the marginal stochastic setting it obtains a rate of $\widetilde O(\sqrt T)$, and for piecewise-stationary means with $J$ segments its rate is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{JT})$. More generally, the rate depends on a threshold-complexity measure of the predictable mean process relative to the group family. We show that this dependence is tight up to logarithmic factors.
core_methodology: The paper introduces an online multicalibration algorithm that dynamically adapts to the difficulty of the prediction sequence by refining a dyadic grid. It achieves worst-case optimal performance while also adapting to easier stochastic or piecewise-stationary environments. The complexity is measured by a threshold-complexity measure of the predictable mean process.
data_sources: The abstract does not specify a particular data source. However, it could be applied to any time-series data where accurate probability calibration is important, such as predicted probabilities of price movements.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improved risk management and bet sizing. If the algorithm can provide more accurately calibrated probability estimates of price movements (e.g., confidence intervals), it could lead to more efficient risk allocation and optimized betting strategies, particularly in volatile or regime-switching markets. Better calibration improves decision-making under uncertainty, making strategies more robust against unexpected price swings.

title: LLM Agents Already Know When to Call Tools -- Even Without Reasoning
summary: Tool-augmented LLM agents tend to call tools indiscriminately, even when the model can answer directly. Each unnecessary call wastes API fees and latency, yet no existing benchmark systematically studies when a tool call is actually needed. We propose When2Tool, a benchmark of 18 environments (15 single-hop, 3 multi-hop) spanning three categories of tool necessity -- computational scale, knowledge boundaries, and execution reliability -- each with controlled difficulty levels that create a clear decision boundary between tool-necessary and tool-unnecessary tasks. We evaluate two families of training-free baselines: Prompt-only (varying the prompt to discourage unnecessary calls) and Reason-then-Act (requiring the model to reason about tool necessity before acting). Both provide limited control: Prompt-only suppresses necessary calls alongside unnecessary ones, and Reason-then-Act still incurs a disproportionate accuracy cost on hard tasks. To understand why these baselines fail, we probe the models' hidden states and find that tool necessity is linearly decodable from the pre-generation representation with AUROC 0.89--0.96 across six models, substantially exceeding the model's own verbalized reasoning. This reveals that models already know when tools are needed, but fail to act on this knowledge during generation. Building on this finding, we propose Probe&Prefill, which uses a lightweight linear probe to read the hidden-state signal and prefills the model's response with a steering sentence. Across all models tested, Probe&Prefill reduces tool calls by 48% with only 1.7% accuracy loss, while the best baseline at comparable accuracy only reduces 6% of tool calls, or achieves a similar tool call reduction but incurs a 5$\times$ higher accuracy loss. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/when2tool
core_methodology: The paper focuses on improving the efficiency of Large Language Model (LLM) agents by reducing unnecessary tool calls. It introduces a benchmark (When2Tool) to evaluate when a tool call is truly needed, and proposes a method called Probe&Prefill, which uses a linear probe to read the hidden-state signal of the LLM and steer the response, reducing tool calls with minimal accuracy loss. The core innovation lies in identifying and acting upon the LLM's implicit understanding of tool necessity before explicit reasoning.
data_sources: The paper doesn't directly use financial data. However, the benchmark involves diverse tasks spanning computational scale, knowledge boundaries, and execution reliability, which could potentially be adapted to simulate financial agent workflows involving market data retrieval, analysis, and order execution.
alpha_potential: While not directly generating alpha, the methodology could improve the cost-efficiency and latency of LLM-powered trading agents. By minimizing unnecessary API calls for data fetching or analysis, agents can respond more quickly to market changes and execute trades more efficiently, especially in high-frequency or automated trading scenarios. Furthermore, more efficient agent architectures could make complex, model-driven trading strategies viable by reducing infrastructure and compute demands.

title: Fast Rates for Offline Contextual Bandits with Forward-KL Regularization under Single-Policy Concentrability
summary: \emph{Kullback-Leibler} (KL) regularization is ubiquitous in reinforcement learning algorithms in the form of \emph{reverse} or \emph{forward} KL. Recent studies have demonstrated $ε^{-1}$-type fast rates for decision making under reverse KL regularization, in contrast to the standard $ε^{-2}$-type sample complexity. However, for forward-KL-regularized objectives, existing statistical analyses are either not applicable or result in $\tilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ slow rates. We take the first step towards addressing this problem via a streamlined analysis of forward-KL-regularized offline CBs. We give the first $\tilde{O}(ε^{-1})$ upper bounds in tabular and general function approximation settings, both under notions of \emph{single-policy concentrability}. In particular, our convex-analytical pipeline unifies these settings by exploiting the pessimism principle in a novel way and completely bypasses the proof routines in previous works based on the mean value theorem, which might be of independent interest. Moreover, we provide rate-optimal lower bounds, manifesting the tightness of our upper bounds in terms of statistical rates. Our lower bounds also demonstrate that the forward-KL-regularized sample complexity recovers the unregularized slow rate in the low-regularization regime, similarly to the reverse-KL regularization.
core_methodology: The paper focuses on offline contextual bandits (CBs) with forward-KL regularization, aiming to improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning. It develops a convex-analytical pipeline based on the pessimism principle to achieve faster convergence rates (ε⁻¹) under single-policy concentrability assumptions, compared to existing slower rates (ε⁻²). It also provides rate-optimal lower bounds, demonstrating the tightness of its upper bounds.
data_sources: The paper is theoretical and does not explicitly mention specific data sources, but it targets applications where offline data is available, implying historical market data could be used in a trading context, but also alternative data that can be cast as a contextual bandit problem.
alpha_potential: The potential alpha arises from improved decision-making in dynamic trading environments. By efficiently learning from historical data and optimizing trading policies, the approach could identify profitable trading opportunities more quickly and accurately than traditional methods. The faster convergence rates offered by forward-KL regularization may lead to quicker adaptation to changing market dynamics and better portfolio allocation decisions. Trading applications in automated order-book execution, dynamic risk management, or option pricing are feasible.

title: Practical Scaling Laws: Converting Compute into Performance in a Data-Constrained World
summary: The scaling laws guiding modern model training were calibrated for a single regime: data-rich, single-epoch pretraining. The dominant such scaling law form, Chinchilla's $L = E + A/N^α+ B/D^β$, has three structural limitations outside that regime: it diverges as unique data shrinks instead of saturating at the uninformed baseline; it cannot represent overfitting when capacity exceeds the data; and it conflates total examples seen with unique examples available. We propose a closed-form extension, $L(N, D, T) = E + (L_0 - E)\,h/(1+h)$ with $h = a/N^α+ b/T^β+ c\,N^γ/D^δ$, that decomposes loss into undercapacity, undertraining, and overfitting terms. It saturates between the irreducible loss $E$ and an uninformed baseline $L_0$ fixed by the loss type, and reduces to Chinchilla in the data-rich, single-epoch limit. We validate it on four multi-epoch experiments spanning four architecture families (MLPs, ResNets, Fourier neural operators, and transformers) across vision, scientific ML, and language domains, and refit it to five published LLM scaling-law grids. Extrapolating to higher compute and larger unique data than seen at fit time, our form achieves state-of-the-art RMSE on every published LLM grid we evaluate and on most cells of our constructed experiments. Once calibrated, the form admits a cost-aware allocation that recovers Chinchilla's optimum when data is free and shifts toward smaller corpora and more epochs as data grows expensive.
core_methodology: The paper proposes an improved scaling law for model performance, specifically addressing limitations of the Chinchilla scaling law in data-constrained scenarios. It introduces a new closed-form equation that decomposes loss into undercapacity, undertraining, and overfitting components. The methodology involves fitting this new scaling law to experimental data across different architecture families and domains, and demonstrating its superior extrapolation capabilities to larger compute and data scales. It ultimately suggest an optimal allocation of compute and data towards model training.
data_sources: The paper uses pretraining data across vision, scientific ML, and language domains, including data used in published LLM scaling-law grids. The specific datasets are not explicitly named, but they are assumed to be standard datasets used for training MLPs, ResNets, Fourier neural operators and transformers.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the ability to more accurately extrapolate model performance for financial time series forecasting. By using the more accurate scaling law, quants can optimize the compute allocation for training models (e.g., LSTMs, Transformers) on financial data with limited historical data, leading to better performing models at a lower cost. This is especially relevant in less liquid markets where historical data is scarce, or when using alternative data with limited history. This optimal allocation can improve model performance at same computational budget.

title: Agentic MIP Research: Accelerated Constraint Handler Generation
summary: Mixed-integer programming (MIP) research is both mathematically sophisticated and engineering-intensive: testing an algorithmic hypothesis within a branch-and-cut solver requires substantial implementation, debugging, tuning, and large-scale benchmarking. We propose an agentic MIP research framework that shortens this feedback loop by embedding LLM agents into a solver-aware harness for generating, verifying, and evaluating plugins for the open-source solver SCIP. Propagation methods play a central role in accelerating MIP solving by exploiting global constraints. We instantiate our framework on the semantic lifting of MIP formulations into global constraints and the automatic construction of propagation-only SCIP constraint handlers. On the MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set, the framework successfully recovers global constraint structures from constraint programming and generates executable constraint detectors and propagation-only constraint handlers. Furthermore, the framework naturally extends to in-context learning within a sandboxed environment, enabling agents not only to tune and debug generated constraint handlers on real instances, but also to explore global constraint patterns in MIP problems and discover novel propagation strategies not yet implemented in SCIP. This framework allows us to systematically distinguish meaningful algorithmic improvements from low-value or overly costly candidates: the novel propagation methods successfully solved five additional instances within the explored benchmark. Overall, this framework demonstrates that LLM agents can autonomously navigate the complex MIP research loop, paving the way for a more automated solver development process.
core_methodology: The paper proposes an agentic framework using LLMs to automatically generate and evaluate constraint handlers for mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers (SCIP). Specifically, it focuses on semantically lifting MIP formulations into global constraints and automatically constructing propagation-only constraint handlers. The LLM agents are used to generate, tune, and debug these handlers within a sandboxed environment.
data_sources: MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set (a standard dataset for evaluating MIP solvers)
alpha_potential: While not directly applicable to financial data, improved MIP solvers can indirectly enhance portfolio optimization and algorithmic trading strategies that heavily rely on integer programming for complex constraints and combinatorial optimization tasks. This speedup can unlock previously intractable strategies or improve the efficiency of existing ones by allowing for faster rebalancing and strategy adjustment.
